utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, but the answer was not very audible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, as you may have heard, I have to put the question again to you because the interpreters could not receive your response. Could you speak a little loudly, please. My question to you was that: Were there other barracks in which members of the platoon of the military police company of the operations group Bosanska Krajina was located, and I suggested to you that there might have been at the JNA barracks, Orasac, and you responded. Could you please give us your answer again?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: My answer was no, because members of the military police company were only billeted in the former JNA centre in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now as to your role or as to the role of the military police, you indicated to us that amongst the role was investigations, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. preparing them to write reports, et cetera. My question to you with respect to your role is, when crimes were reported by victims, exactly how did the military police go about investigating such crimes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If a victim reported a crime committed by army members, that is to say by soldiers, we would then go to carry out an on-site investigation to secure the site, and if the perpetrator was known, we would arrest the perpetrator, question the perpetrator, the suspect. We would file a criminal report and forward the case to the relevant prosecutor's office. If the perpetrator or perpetrators were unknown, then as a rule we acted together with the civilian police, because we did not know who the perpetrator was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now with respect to the JNA barracks in particular. Is it your testimony that under your command the military police company of the operations group Bosnia Krajina had never received reports of any kind from either victims, civilians, or families of victims with respect to mistreatment of POWs at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I as the commander of the MP company never received any complaints from the detainees themselves or from their family members or from the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But you will agree with me if I say to you that members of your platoon guarded the detention centre at the JNA barracks? You would agree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. My policemen secured part of the military detention unit, not the prison, only part of the military detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Your members had absolutely nothing to do with respect to the protection of the POWs at the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Excuse me. That's what I am asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: My MPs secured the military detention unit, and in one part of it, when we had POWs, that's where they were located, in the detention unit. That's where they were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So in fact, they were guarded by your military police, the POWs, whilst they were in the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As far as you know, you had never received any complaints from the POWs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to reports received, were the military police able to address requests received from the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. You said criminal reports and then you mentioned an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: My colleague showed you a group of documents in your language, starting off number 1328 and following, and you indicated to the Court that you based your investigations on requests received. Am I correct so far?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We carried out our investigations until criminal reports were filed, and we did this independently. But if we filed a criminal report and handed it over to the prosecutor's office, we then only acted upon requests from the prosecutor's office if there were any questions, and if not, we didn't hand anything over.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I think we're on the same page. A little bit further than that I'm asking now with respect to requests from investigating judges, did you instigate investigations if a request came in from an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If the investigating judge asked us to carry out certain investigations on the ground with respect to a particular crime, we would do that as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So my question to you, then, were that if -- was if you had received requests with respect to complaints that were made to, for example, an investigating judge, and you were asked to carry out certain examinations, was your department -- was that part of the role that your department played?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Firstly, we never sent our reports to the judge. Our reports were sent to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I understand you, but my question is: Should an investigating judge request of you to do an investigation, was that in the preamble of your duties? Could you carry it out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If an investigating judge asked us to carry out certain actions to add to what had already been done by ourselves during our initial investigation, we would do that, and we would send him a report on our additional findings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thanks. Would you consider -- or, rather, could you tell us what was the life of the -- of the unit? For how long did this unit exist?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: The unit existed from the 26th of June, 1993, up to sometime in April or May 1994. At that moment, the new corps was established, the 7th Corps, and a new military police unit was established to be attached to the new corps. That was the 7th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you indicated in your examination-in-chief that you worked along or you cooperated with the civilian police. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What about reports that may have been made to the civilian police? Were you involved in investigating such complaints?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody filed a direct report to the civilian police, and if they felt the need for our help or if they thought that the perpetrators were members of the military, then we cooperated and carried out certain parts of the investigation together.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you had ever received reports from the civilian police with respect to reports that had been made been civilians with respect to mistreatment of POWs or detainees in the JNA barracks? Did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I never received a single report from the civilian police to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Document 1603 was shown to you, and it's a register of reports, numerous reports, and when I looked through the report and when I looked through the document, all the reports are basically of a similar nature, and maybe you can explain to the Trial Chamber for us a little bit about how it operated. Most of the -- most of the reports are simple theft, larceny of a car, a pig, or something of that sort, that nature. Did you ever receive any serious reports with respect to looting in your AOR?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: All events that were reported to the MP company were individual cases, and that is why they were qualified as such. When you say "looting," what I have in mind is an organised group of people acting in concert and stealing things from a large number of buildings, taking everything that they can put their hands on. The crimes committed were threats and aggravated threats. There was no looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At no time at all in your tenure always commander of the military police company of the operations group Bosanska Krajina, at no time at all did you ever receive or any reports were received with respect to members of your platoon breaking into houses, stealing equipment, destroying houses? At no time at all? Of course in your AOR.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Members of my platoon of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, of the military, of the army. No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 50, line 16, the witness said that there was theft and aggravated theft, and my colleagues are telling me that the word used is threats. I am not sure that this word means the same. Can this please be corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has been done. You may proceed, Ms. Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Members of the army. And if I made a mistake I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: There were reports against members of the military who were stealing things from a -- individual houses. We acted on such reports immediately. If they were found on the spot, they were arrested, taken Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. into custody. They were interrogated as suspects and criminal reports were filed against them. If the owner of the stolen property was there, then the stolen property was returned to such an owner. If the owner wasn't there, then the stolen property was stored in a place that was envisaged for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thanks. Did you -- you were in contact with the civilian police, and you worked along with them. What about the civilian prosecutor? Did you have a working relationship with the civilian prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have any contact with his office because there was no need for me to have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And how was the punishment that was given out to the perpetrators, who prescribed the punishment?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the type of crime committed. There were some disciplinary breaches that could be punished by the commander. The disciplinary measures could be instituted by the commander. If a crime was committed, then the military police filed the criminal report to the prosecutor's office. The prosecutor's office forwarded that report to the court and such a criminal would be tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And was it your duty or was it the role of the military police company of the operations group Bosanska Krajina to follow up on these reports?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not my duty to follow that. My duty was to file my criminal reports to the proper place, and to be honest, I didn't have the time to do anything else. It was war.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And the proper place would have been to whom, to which department?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say forward to the proper place? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I am responding to what you responded, and maybe I can quote you. You said that, "My duty was to file my criminal reports to the proper place," and I asked you where was the proper place or who was the proper place.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: The relevant military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And now I go back to my question. If -- if the report was filed to the relevant military prosecutor's office and no action was done, do you follow up the report to see if it was, in fact, sent? Did you follow it up? Did your department follow up the report to see what action was given to the report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Once we submitted our criminal report to the military prosecutor's office, the military prosecutor made his own assessment as to whether the criminal report contained enough elements for criminal proceedings. If there were not enough such elements, the criminal record could be rejected. I didn't have either the time or possibility to follow my criminal report to the prosecutor's office and onwards in the court. I didn't do that. I didn't have the time or the capability to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You would agree with me, I take it, that there is the possibility that the report could end up on a desk and never be seen by the military prosecutor and that's the end of the matter? You agree with me that that could happen?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't. Every criminal report was made out in two copies. When it was received by the prosecutor's office, it was registered when the criminal report was received, on what date by the prosecutor's office, and this was on both copies, on the copies that remained with the prosecutor and on the copies that were -- on the copy that was returned to me, to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You see, I ask you this question because one of your -- your duties is the pre-trial investigation of the -- of the criminal offences. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And it was in that vein that I posed question to you that if the matter was not followed up by your department.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the general tone of the investigations? How were these investigations carried out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as we either received information or notice that certain crimes had been or were being committed, military policemen from my company would be sent to secure the place of crime. We had people who were involved in investigations, and these people would inform the prosecutor and the judge, and they could go with us to the crime scene or they could authorise somebody else to carry out an on-spot investigation. It depended on the gravity of the crime. In keeping with our technical capabilities and equipment, and those that we used belonged to the public security station because we did not have our own, we would mark the traces of crime. We would carry out an on-site investigation. We would interview witnesses or eyewitnesses, if there were any, in order to collect as much information as possible as to who the perpetrator of the crime might be. If the perpetrator had been recognised by somebody, we established their identity and we tried to locate them to arrest them and to bring them in. On our premises these persons would be interrogated as suspects and criminal reports would be filed against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I look at the time and I wonder if this would be a convenient time for us to take the break. I do not anticipate I will be much longer when we get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is twenty-five to six. We are going to make a break until five to six or 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to Mrs. Benjamin again.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have two questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated to us in your testimony in examination-in-chief that you reported to the commander of the OG as well as sometimes to the assistant for military security. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I was directly responsible to the commander of the OG when it came to the police task and duties. I had indirect contact via the assistant commander for security with the commander when the latter was absent. And also from the assistant commander for security, I received professional and expert advice on my work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there were any instances of looting, for example, by soldiers, the assistant for military security could be informed, and he could have knowledge of same. Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Things like that never happened, and that's why I never had to report to him on any such thing. However, through my report on the work of the MP company which I submitted to him on a daily basis, I informed him about everything that was happening on the ground and what was done by the company of the military police with that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And my last question to you is you had stated -- made reserve to the military police battalion and the military police company, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you give us the distinction between the military police battalion and the military police company, if there is any?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a difference. An MP company is a smaller military unit, and it has a hundred or up to 120 military policemen at the most. A battalion and the company can both be on the strength on motorised brigades which were bigger formations within the BiH army. A battalion is a bigger military police unit which consists of at least five companies, so a battalion should be five times bigger than a company. It has a battalion command. It has its commander who has his assistants. It is an independent military police unit that acts within a corps, which is the highest formation within the structure of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: You worked along with the civilian police. Would I be correct in saying that you also worked along with the military police battalion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: You would be right when it came to my professional and expert equipment. A battalion was a figurer formation, and they received Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. instructions from their higher command, and according to that instruction, if I needed any professional or expert help, then they would be instructed to help me or I would address them for help, and in that respect we cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the end of the cross-examination. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menkovic, my learned friend asked you about crimes that you detected, elucidated and reported, and she asked you about looting. In your answers you gave us a number of examples of theft and aggravated theft. If anything else happened at the time, if any other crime had been committed by army members, crimes such as murder or a similar thing, would you have acted in the same way you acted in case of arson or theft?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: The approach was identical to all the committed crimes. We focused and invested a lot of effort in detecting perpetrators of aggravated crimes. This can be seen from my documents that I sent to the prosecutor's office, especially in my reports that involved aggravated crimes, bodily injury, murders and similar things. Luckily enough, we managed to detect perpetrators of all the aggravated crimes, and we managed to refer those criminals to the prosecutor's office and further on to the courts for trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were a platoon commander in a brigade, and later on you became the commander of a company within an OG. My learned friend suggested a time period preceding the establishment of that company, and you answered her. In the brigades, not only in yours but in others as well, were there military police platoons that were engaged in the tasks and duties that you testified about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Every mountain brigade by its military formation and by its organisation had to have a Military Police Platoon on its strength. A motorised brigade, which is a bigger formation, according to its formation had to have a military police company on its strength.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, Mr. Menkovic, when the military police company of the OG was established, did the platoons and the company on the strength of the motorised brigade remain existing within those units and did they continue performing their duties within the purview of their respective brigades?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They continued functioning on the strength of their respective brigades. The objective of the formation of the military company of the Bosanska Krajina OG was to establish such a unit that could go beyond the boundaries of the area of responsibility of any one brigade. They could work across the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When it came to detecting crimes and perpetrators of those crimes, can you tell us what was the position of the commander of the OG of the 3rd Corps? Were you told by your commander that you had to detect criminals, or if you hadn't done that, would they have tolerated that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I could not fail to act on criminal reports filed. From the moment the 3rd Corps was established, one could feel a certain change in the work of the brigades and especially in the military police platoons. A pressure was put on brigade commanders to mobilise into those units only those people who would be the best suited to become military policemen. A pressure was put from the top town the line which said that our men had to be trained in order to respond to our task in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is a mistake on line -- on page 57, line 25 and page 58, line 1. My question was the commander of the OG and the commander of the 3rd Corps, and here it reads as if the OG equals the 3rd Corps. I apologise for the interruption. I had to make the correction while the page was still before me. You have answered my question, but I have an additional question to put to you. Did the commander of the OG, who was your superior officer as you've told us, or anybody else, any other of your superior commanders, did they ever ask you or tell you not to perform your duty, not to detect a certain crime although it would have been normal for you to do that within the purview of your duties?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: On the contrary. The commander always insisted on crime prevention. He insisted on preventing crimes committed by BiH members. There were never any attempts to obstruct my work and the work of the military police. Pressure was always exerted on us to perform those duties and carry out those tasks to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The position of the OG commander, was it in accordance with the policies of the 3rd Corps Command with regard to detecting and prosecuting perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the previous answer, I said that when the corps was established, we noticed that discipline was being tightened up and that we had more work and we were performing this work better. These are only orders that could have come from the commander, especially from the 3rd Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague asked you a number of questions about the work of the prosecution and the court and on whether you followed their work. Tell me whether at any point in time in 1993 in the course of the war did the military police or military unit, a brigade, an operations group, or a corps, did they ever have authority over the courts or the prosecution's office are or, rather, were the prosecution and the court military organs or judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor's office, the military prosecutor's office, the military court were always independent of the army, and they were always under the civilian authorities in those areas. As far as I know, that was the case, and I was there throughout that period, but as far as I know, the army was never responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the large number of criminal reports that you filed with the prosecutor's office or, rather, with the court, do you know whether Commander Alagic and brigade commanders were ever unhappy about the expeditiousness of the procedures engaged or were there any complaints or reports that were drafted or is there nothing that you know about this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether from the superior command drafted documents in which they expressed their discontent, because dealing with court proceedings was too slow, but I had some unpleasant experiences with commanders from brigade units in which the policemen were subordinated to me. Because there were forces engaged in combat, but if someone had done something, we would detain the person. We would arrest the person. And they felt uneasy because of this, because the proceedings in court were too slow. The courts or the court needed at least six months to deal with a case, and in some situations cases would go on for a year or even more, and in some situations cases were never resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to ask the witness my following question, could he be shown DH119. Could you give the B/C/S to the -- the B/C/S version to the witness. Mr. Menkovic, as you can see, this document is a report only the work of the district military prosecutor's office in Travnik for 1993. Do you have the document before you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Do you have the report on the district military prosecutor's office for 1993, because perhaps there is a mistake. Is that what it says in the heading?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We thought that we made a mistake as far as the number, it was listed under as concerned. With regard to the questions by my learned friend on whether reports remained on the prosecutor's desk, could you have a look on page 2, item 2. Could you read out what it says there? Number 2, item 2.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: "Criminal reports received. The prosecutor's office in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reporting period received a total of 823 criminal reports against 1.044 individuals."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, does this report show that you submitted a large number of criminal reports to the prosecutor's office and you had proof of that in your archives where one copy of your report or reports were kept?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the following page, page 3, item 4B. My learned friend, since you aren't interested in what happened to criminal reports, my learned friend asked you whether criminal reports might remain on the desk of the prosecutor without having anything done about them. Have a look at item 4B and could you please read is out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Six hundred eighty-eight requests were made to conduct an investigation against 860 individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this information show how many criminal reports were filed by the MPs and other organs, and does it show -- how much such requests were dealt with by the prosecutor's office or, rather, does it show how many requests they made for the relevant organs to conduct investigations against certain individuals?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what these figures show.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In an area such as the area covered by the district military court or, rather, the district military prosecutor's office in Travnik, what would you say? Was this a small, significant, or very large number of -- of criminal reports that the prosecutor's office dealt with, criminal reports against army members?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Given that this took place in 1993 when the ABiH was fighting a war on two fronts and when each and every soldier was needed, I would say that this number is an extremely high number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Menkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the other Defence team have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a few questions I would like to put to you to clarify certain matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago you said that your company had been established in the AOR of the OG in order to unify the practice or the work of the various platoons or battalions or, rather, companies within brigades. What I would like to know is how did you coordinate your work between the company that you were in command of and the military police of brigades? Let's take one example. The 306th Brigade had its military police force. What did you do or how did you proceed in order to coordinate with them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me. I said that my company was composed of three platoons. I as the company commander was in charge of that unit and of its three platoons, and the purpose of establishing an MP company was to have one unit which could take military and police measures throughout the territory covered by the OG. My task, in accordance with the order on establishing the company, was to help, to train MPs in the existing units and brigades. So I had no authority over them. I couldn't issue them orders. I couldn't order them to do anything, only their commander could. I was only to provide them with professional assistance as far as training is concerned, but if I engaged in action with the company MP in the zone of responsibility of a certain brigade, then I only had to inform the commander in charge of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have understood you very well, but what I wanted to know is the following: Let's take the example of an offence committed by a soldier from the 312th Brigade. In the case of such an offence, would the military police of the 312th deal with such an offence or would you deal with the offence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the MP of the 312th Brigade would deal with it if they were aware of the identity of the perpetrator. But if crimes had been committed, serious crimes in particular, in such a case the military police and the military security service from the company and from the brigade would act together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be more specific, because I really don't understand what you're saying. I provided you with an example. I mentioned a soldier from the 312th who had committed an offence, who would be involved in the proceedings and who would send a report to the military prosecutor. Would it be the commander of the 312th or would this be done through the commander of the OG and in such a case would you send a report to the prosecutor? Who would send the report?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If the report on the crime was sent to the MP company, we would immediately do everything that was necessary. MPs from the company would do this. But if the event was reported to the military police of the 312th, then this depended on what was necessary. If they could carry out the investigation on their own, then they would do so. They had there right. But if they were not in a position to do it on their own, we would assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case of an offence, you said that you were under General Alagic. Did you correspond with General Alagic orally or did you submit written reports? How did you report to your superior? Did you tell him tell him orally this is what is happening, that is what I'm going to do or were you obliged to send a written report to say you were going to hand over the case to the military prosecutor's office? Who took the final decision, you or General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I drafted daily written reports on the work of the MP company. I did this through my operations officer who was on duty 24 hours a day. So any event reported to the operations centre was recorded, and I would inform my superior command of the relevant information in a written report. As far as the decision on submitting criminal reports is concerned, well, this was a decision I had to take, because if we had established through investigations that there was -- there were reasonable grounds to suspect that someone had committed a crime, I, or rather, my service would draft a criminal report which would I -- which I would sign and then send to the prosecutor's office. And in this written report there would be information on the perpetrators of a certain crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you would file a criminal report with the military prosecutor. General Alagic didn't play a role at this stage.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean as far as filing criminal reports are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And you said that you would sign. Would General Alagic also sign these criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the very beginning when the MP company was being established and before I received the official stamps. There were a few cases of that kind, and then I was authorised by the general to sign criminal reports on my own. I was given such authority as the commander of the MP company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when did you obtain such authorisation? When did you obtain this right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you have a look at a document in the binder provided to you by the Defence, under section 4, criminal report, tab 6. Tab 6. There's a report to the prosecutor dated the 14th of July, 1993. This report concerns Dervis Colo. Can you see? Did you find the document?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, it's a report, a criminal report against Dervis Colo, dated the 14th of July and signed by Alagic. Why didn't you sign this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but perhaps I was absent, or perhaps at this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time I had not yet received his authorisation to sign criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another minor question. In this report, as you can see, there's a date, the 14th of July, and there's a number above it. This is at the top to the left and it says 09/10-2. That's a -- handwritten. Isn't there a mistake there? Isn't there a number 2 that's missing after the 9? Shouldn't it be 092/10-2?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the number under which it was recorded. As to whether this number is correct, I don't know. I couldn't say. It should be the 9th criminal report recorded, and then it says "/ -- -2".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have a look at the next page. Have a look at page 3. This is a special report sent on the 15th of February, and at the top to the left there's a stamp and it says 092/10-2.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you provide us with an explanation? Why is there a stamp there, and why wasn't it typewritten?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is probably when you're producing a stamp which could be used instead of the heading on the document that was being forwarded. In this case we didn't have it, so -- so we typed it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the stamp there, it was stamped on the 15th of February, 1994. So in February 1994, you did have such a stamp.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did have a stamp. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good evening, Witness. I have two or three questions on the military police to put to you in relation to military operations. In the course of military operations, villages may be taken by the army, conquered on the HVO forces for instance, and my question to you is what exactly is the situation of the military police and especially your unit in relation towards ongoing military operations? Are you present with your military police as part of your military police presence at the front line? Does it follow the movements of the front line? Could you tell us something in general about your presence at the front line, especially when the front line is moving?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If there's an order from the competent commander according to which the entire unit or part of it has been engaged in combat, then we would be present. We would also be involved in the combat. But if a unit wasn't being engaged in combat, we would only go into action after the active troops had passed through the territory, and in such orders there was always an order as to what the military police had to do in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you as a military police, unless you take yourself part in the military actions, you are on stand-by so to speak. If a village has been taken, you come in and you fulfil your tasks. Is that a correct understanding of what you said?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: In the combat order from the commander, we would be assigned the tasks we had to carry out in a given village. For example, ensure that no one entered the village without authorisation. That would be a matter of priority. If there were POWs, we'd have to take them over from the troops or, rather, from the security service that had interrogated them, for example. And if any inhabitants remained, then we should make sure that they were safe in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That is exactly the kind of things I wanted to know from you, your presence at the front line after a village has been taken or after some territorial gains have been made by the army. Let me also put you some more specific questions. We know or we heard that we say that in June in the Bila valley a number of villages have been taken by the army, villages like Maline or Cukle or other villages. Do you have any remembrance of your unit being there at the time, at the beginning of June, and doing the work that military police normally do? Can you remember a specific period in June that you were active in that field?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the time period. However, neither me nor my unit were present there. At that time, I was still on the strength of the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So there was not yet a unified operation groups. I understand that was the 16th or 17th of July. That is correct? But in your capacity at that time, on the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade, were you protecting houses against looting, or houses against burning, or arson, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: On the axis of action of the 17th Krajina Mountain Brigade, we did our police work, whatever was required from us. If we did not participate directly in combat operations, we did everything that could prevent theft, looting, arson, or any other illegal acts. This is what we military policemen on the strength of the 17th Krajina Brigade did, but we did it only on the axis of action of our brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What parts -- I'm sorry. What part of the region there was the 17th Krajina Brigade engaged in? Could you name some villages that were in the area of activities of the 17th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: The 17th Krajina Brigade had three infantry battalions on its strength. It is very difficult for me to remember certain axes where they were active, because I did not participate directly in any combat. However, from the commander, I received a task to secure or to try and prevent certain crimes in the area north from Travnik, and the villages that I can remember now after 13 years are Bilici, Ovcarevo, Paklarevo, the area towards Turbe, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If there has been a movement of the front line and new areas have been conquered and there's, as you've said, a need to protect villages that have been abandoned by the inhabitants, how long are you staying there? What is the time span of your presence in these situations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the end of combat operations, the priority task of the military police was to try and protect those villages. However, those who had to protect those areas were the civilian police and the civilian protection. The civilian protection, as an institution, they didn't carry arms, you know. That is why we came to help out. We could not be there all the time to protect the abandoned property around the clock, because there were problems elsewhere, and we had other tasks and duties. We did try, however, to send our patrols to the abandoned villages and to cooperate with the public security station in order to help the civilian population and to protect the abandoned areas as best as we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'm turning to the Prosecution. Are there any questions arising from the Judges' questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, there won't be any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the Defence the same. Do they want to ask any questions arising from the Judges' questioning in order to clarify any of the answers?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menkovic, you said the commander didn't have to give you any particular consent for you to file a criminal report. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to my question, you mentioned the regulations and laws that set out your authorities. I would then ask you, was it the law that gave you the right and obligation to file criminal reports once you collected enough information about the perpetrator or the crime and that nobody had to give you any particular authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure regulated the duties of the military police, and by that law I was duty-bound to investigate crimes, to elucidate crimes, and to file criminal reports. If I had not filed criminal reports, I would have disobeyed the law that was in effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When this came to your commander, you said earlier that your authorities arose from the orders issued by your superior commander. Within the performance of your duties, did your commander issue orders to you to institute measures in order to prevent crimes and to prosecute perpetrators of crimes? Was that the commander's role in respect of the military police? Did the commander have any other authorities with respect to the military police?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: If there was no combat going on, all the subordinate officers had briefings with their superior commander. At every of these briefings, pressure was put on me to step up the military police activities in order to prevent crimes and other illegal activities in the area, the area in which property was completely unprotected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the questions of the Trial Chamber, you mentioned the authorities that you had in your respective brigades and you provided us with a very good explanation of that. Did you have to instruct the platoons of the military police to file criminal reports or did they have to do it by virtue of their position and work?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever happened in the area of their responsibility, they had to file reports on within the purview of their responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the rate of crime and the abandoned area, did your presence in the territory covered by certain brigades meant that there were less crimes committed by army members, or was your presence there the presence of somebody who had authority in the area?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you that we were established in order to step up activities in the zone and to reduce the rate of crime as much as possible. Our presence in itself in any of the brigades had a positive effect on the brigade military police, because our role was to educate them and to give them any sort of assistance that we could provide them with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menkovic, a commander is the highest authority, and a commander has his bodies such as the Military Police Platoon. Given his position, is the commander in the position to sign any document issued by any of the units subordinated to him if he believes that he should do so?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked about your authorities with regard to combat operations, and you said that your roles primarily arose from the orders of the commander who planned such an operation. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have also said that this was determined by the axis of action of the unit that the military police was on the strength of. You know that the front line moved very often. Were your tasks relative to following the front line of your unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. As the front line moved, the military police unit would follow -- would follow its brigade. However, my unit was rather independent, and I had to receive specific tasks from my commander as to how I should follow my brigade and what my specific tasks were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you had responsibility to detect crimes committed by military personnel, can you tell me, according to the law which was in effect throughout the war, which body was responsible for the safety and security of citizens, territory, and property, and who was it who had the primary task to do that in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: It was the civilian police, public security stations. They were the ones who had the primary task to look after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally I would like to ask as follows: As commander of the military police company acting on the axis of the 17th Krajina Brigade and later only the commander of the company of the military police of the OG, did you ever, during any combat operations, did you ever face wilful destruction of property and wilful arson of houses committed by members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN MENKOVIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions from us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, your testimony is finished. You have provided answers to the Defence, to the Prosecution, and to the Judges. I would like to thank you for coming here to The Hague to testify. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish you a happy journey back home. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom, and once again, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to turn to the Defence. I would like to know whether they have any documents to tender into evidence, or maybe we can do tomorrow if it is too complicated to do it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is exactly what I was going to ask you. There are a number of documents that have to be marked for identification, and I would very much like to do it tomorrow rather than today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It is going to be tomorrow afternoon because our session is in the afternoon tomorrow at 2.15, and I would like to invite all of you to come back to the courtroom tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of January, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
